summary:
In microgravity, the loss of the human body's hydrostatic gradient causes a massive headward fluid shift. This creates a lymphatic drainage bottleneck, elevating Intracranial Pressure (ICP) and compressing the optic nerve. This cascade results in Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), a critical risk for space missions leading to progressive vision loss.
NASA currently relies on low interval OCT scans which detect structural damage after it happens and require Earth-based doctors for analysis. We shift the approach from reactive imaging to constant predictive functional diagnostics. Using daily passive checks, such as “MoonFace” detection while looking in a mirror,  as well as a targeted interactive vision test. Our algorithm tracks early functional biomarkers, for example, color and contrast sensitivity degradation, to reverse-engineer and estimate ICP levels before irreversible structural deformation occurs.
Designed for deep space, the system requires zero payload weight, operating entirely on existing onboard hardware (standard tablets) or an easy to install supportive system. It is 100% autonomous, providing real-time, on-device analysis that bypasses the 20-minute Earth communication delay as much as possible.
V&V and Earth Application:
The system's algorithm provides a clear Verification and Validation pathway using easy to use tests and a use of clinical OCT and visual field data from terrestrial glaucoma patients if needed.
details:
EYERIS: Project Details

The problem: In weightlessness, about 2 litres of fluid shifts toward the head. About 66% of long-duration astronauts show early signs of SANS (Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome), such as optic nerve swelling and blurred near vision, and some changes last for years. The ISS has an OCT eye scanner, but scans are weeks apart, so changes can go unnoticed in between.

Our solution: EYERIS is a tablet app astronauts use on their own:

Weekly vision tests (~10 min): blind spot mapping, near acuity, Amsler grid and contrast sensitivity. Each targets a specific SANS sign.

Eye pressure from our pressure-measuring device, plus daily vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂) and a symptom check-in.

Body photo log tracking the visible fluid shift: puffy face, neck veins, “bird legs”.

Personal baseline: each astronaut is compared with their own preflight results, and alerts fire on real change or worsening trends.

Flight surgeon dashboard showing the whole crew’s status and alerts in one view.

Key message: EYERIS doesn’t replace OCT. It’s a cheap, frequent screen between scans that tells the medical team when to scan.

Status: Working prototype with a demo mode. It is not a diagnostic tool. Next steps are direct device connection, real logins, and validation against OCT results.

Biomedical engineering students, Technion – NASA Hackathon
